name: Learn: etcd Restore
objective: CKA › Cluster Architecture, Installation & Configuration (25%). Goal: take an etcd snapshot, inspect it, and restore it into a fresh data directory — the companion to backup and a near-guaranteed exam task.
description: etcd is the single source of truth for a cluster. Learn to snapshot it, verify the snapshot, restore it into a new data directory, and understand how the static etcd Pod would be repointed at that directory — step by step, without ever endangering the live cluster.

questions.title: Take a fresh etcd snapshot
questions.teach:
**etcd** holds all cluster state. A backup is a point-in-time **snapshot** taken with `etcdctl snapshot save`, talking to etcd over TLS with the etcd client certs.

**The three TLS flags (always required):**
- `--cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt` — verifies the server.
- `--cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt` and `--key=.../server.key` — the client identity. (`healthcheck-client.crt/.key` also work.)
- `--endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379` — the client port (2379); **2380** is peer traffic, not for clients.

**Exam gotchas:**
- **`ETCDCTL_API=3`** — mandatory for `snapshot` subcommands. It is the *default* on etcd 3.5+, but on exam/older boxes you may need `ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl ...` explicitly; without it, `snapshot save` fails.
- **Distroless image (kind)** — no shell inside the etcd Pod, so call `etcdctl` *directly* as the exec command, never `sh -c ...`.
- **Where you save matters.** The output file must land on a path you can later reach. The data dir `/var/lib/etcd` is a **hostPath** volume, so writing to `/var/lib/etcd/snap.db` inside the Pod appears at the same path on node `$CP`. Saving to a non-mounted path strands the file inside the ephemeral container.
- On a non-containerized node you would instead run `etcdctl` on the host directly (often as root), reading certs from the same `/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/` directory.

Save to `/var/lib/etcd/snap.db`, then copy it to `/opt/snap.db` on `$CP` as your off-box backup.
questions.prompt:
Take a fresh etcd snapshot and place it at `/opt/snap.db` on node `$CP`.

Save from the etcd Pod to `/var/lib/etcd/snap.db`, then copy it to `/opt/snap.db` on `$CP`.

Target: a non-trivial snapshot file exists at `/opt/snap.db` on `$CP`.
questions.hint: POD=$(kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=etcd -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}'); then `kubectl -n kube-system exec $POD -- etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key snapshot save /var/lib/etcd/snap.db`; finally `docker exec "$CP" cp /var/lib/etcd/snap.db /opt/snap.db`.
questions.solution:
POD=$(kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=etcd -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl -n kube-system exec "$POD" -- etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot save /var/lib/etcd/snap.db
docker exec "$CP" cp /var/lib/etcd/snap.db /opt/snap.db
docker exec "$CP" ls -l /opt/snap.db

verification.description: a non-trivial snapshot exists at /opt/snap.db on $CP

questions.title: Inspect the snapshot
questions.teach:
Before trusting a backup, verify it. `snapshot status <file>` reads the snapshot **locally** — no running etcd needed — and prints its **hash**, **revision**, total keys, size and version.

**etcdctl vs etcdutl (the big version gotcha):**
- Up to etcd **3.5**, `snapshot status` and `snapshot restore` live in **`etcdctl`**.
- From etcd **3.6**, they moved to **`etcdutl`** — the offline maintenance tool — and `etcdctl snapshot status` is deprecated/removed. `etcdutl` is *local-only*: it takes **no** `--endpoints`/TLS flags (it reads a file on disk).
- On the exam, check the etcd version first (`etcd --version` / `etcdctl version`) and pick the right binary. Both `status` and `restore` are offline operations.

**Reading the output:**
- A healthy snapshot shows a **non-zero revision** plus a hash; a truncated/corrupt file errors out.
- `--write-out=table` (goes **before** the subcommand) gives the readable HASH/REVISION/TOTAL KEYS/TOTAL SIZE/VERSION table; `--write-out=json` is scriptable.
- `status` does **not** validate against the live keyspace — it only confirms the file is a well-formed, self-consistent snapshot. Always run it right after taking or receiving a backup.
questions.prompt:
Inspect the snapshot you saved at `/var/lib/etcd/snap.db` using `etcdutl snapshot status` (via the etcd Pod, which can see that mounted path).

Target: the status command succeeds and reports a hash and revision for the snapshot.
questions.hint: POD=$(kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=etcd -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}'); then `kubectl -n kube-system exec $POD -- etcdutl --write-out=table snapshot status /var/lib/etcd/snap.db`. The flag goes before the subcommand for etcdutl's table output.
questions.solution:
POD=$(kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=etcd -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl -n kube-system exec "$POD" -- etcdutl --write-out=table snapshot status /var/lib/etcd/snap.db
# +----------+----------+------------+------------+---------+
# |   HASH   | REVISION | TOTAL KEYS | TOTAL SIZE | VERSION |
# +----------+----------+------------+------------+---------+

verification.description: etcdutl snapshot status succeeds (hash + revision) on the saved snapshot

questions.title: Restore into a NEW data directory
questions.teach:
Restoring **never** overwrites the live data dir. You restore the snapshot into a *fresh, empty* directory with `snapshot restore <file> --data-dir <newdir>`. This rebuilds a complete etcd data tree — crucially a `member/` subdirectory containing `snap/` and `wal/`. **The target dir must not already exist**, or the restore refuses.

**etcdctl (≤3.5) vs etcdutl (≥3.6):** `etcdutl snapshot restore ...` on 3.6+, `etcdctl snapshot restore ...` on 3.5. Restore is **offline and local** — no `--endpoints`/TLS flags needed (you're writing files, not talking to a server).

**Flags that matter for a real multi-node restore (all optional for single-node):**
- `--name` — the member name (must match the node), default `default`.
- `--initial-cluster` and `--initial-advertise-peer-urls` — must match the cluster's peer topology so the restored member rejoins correctly.
- `--initial-cluster-token` — set a fresh token to force a new cluster identity.
- Omit these and the defaults are used; that's fine for a single-member cluster but **wrong for HA** — a classic exam trap.

**Here:** the only etcd binaries live inside the distroless etcd Pod, so run the restore via that Pod and target a path **under the mounted `/var/lib/etcd/`** (e.g. `/var/lib/etcd/etcd-restore`) so the rebuilt tree lands on node `$CP`, safely separate from the live `/var/lib/etcd/member`. The live cluster keeps running the whole time.
questions.prompt:
Restore `/var/lib/etcd/snap.db` into a new data directory `/var/lib/etcd/etcd-restore` (via the etcd Pod). Do NOT touch the live `/var/lib/etcd/member`.

Target: directory `/var/lib/etcd/etcd-restore` exists on `$CP` and contains a `member/` subdirectory.
questions.hint: POD=$(kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=etcd -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}'); then `kubectl -n kube-system exec $POD -- etcdutl snapshot restore /var/lib/etcd/snap.db --data-dir /var/lib/etcd/etcd-restore`. Verify on the host with `docker exec "$CP" ls /var/lib/etcd/etcd-restore/member`.
questions.solution:
POD=$(kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=etcd -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl -n kube-system exec "$POD" -- etcdutl snapshot restore /var/lib/etcd/snap.db --data-dir /var/lib/etcd/etcd-restore
docker exec "$CP" ls -la /var/lib/etcd/etcd-restore/member   # snap/ wal/

verification.description: /var/lib/etcd/etcd-restore exists on $CP with a member/ subdirectory

questions.title: Understand the repoint (do NOT modify the live manifest)
questions.teach:
On a real restore, the final step is to point etcd at the restored directory. etcd is a **static Pod** defined by `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml` on the control-plane node. Inside that file, the `etcd-data` **volume** is a `hostPath` whose `path:` is the live data dir (`/var/lib/etcd`).

**Static Pods — how they behave:**
- Managed by the **kubelet** (via `staticPodPath`, i.e. `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/`), not the apiserver/scheduler. You cannot `kubectl edit`/`delete` them to effect change — edit the **file** on disk.
- The kubelet watches that directory and **recreates the Pod automatically** when the manifest changes; no restart needed. Moving the file out and back in is the standard way to force a bounce.
- The apiserver shows a **mirror Pod** (read-only). Its name is suffixed with the node name (e.g. `etcd-<node>`).

**Two ways to go live on a restore:**
1. Edit `hostPath.path` to point at your restored dir, **or**
2. Leave the path as `/var/lib/etcd` and move the restored `member/` contents into it (stop/clear the old dir first).

**Gotchas:** the `hostPath.path` must exist on the node and hold a valid `member/` tree, or etcd crash-loops and the **apiserver goes down with it** (single-node). On kubeadm, `--data-dir` in the etcd command args must also line up with the volume. **Here you only locate it — do NOT edit the live manifest**, because repointing single-node etcd mid-exercise would bounce the apiserver.

Prove you found it by writing the hostPath path into `/opt/etcd-datadir.txt` on `$CP`.
questions.prompt:
Read `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml` on `$CP`, find the `hostPath.path` of the `etcd-data` volume, and write that path into `/opt/etcd-datadir.txt` on `$CP`. Do NOT modify the manifest.

Target: `/opt/etcd-datadir.txt` on `$CP` contains the etcd-data hostPath (`/var/lib/etcd`).
questions.hint: Inspect it: `docker exec "$CP" cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml` and look under `volumes:` for the `etcd-data` volume's `hostPath.path`. Then record it: `docker exec "$CP" sh -c 'echo /var/lib/etcd > /opt/etcd-datadir.txt'`.
questions.solution:
docker exec "$CP" cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml | grep -A2 'name: etcd-data'
# volumes: ... - hostPath: { path: /var/lib/etcd } name: etcd-data
docker exec "$CP" sh -c 'echo /var/lib/etcd > /opt/etcd-datadir.txt'
docker exec "$CP" cat /opt/etcd-datadir.txt

verification.description: /opt/etcd-datadir.txt holds the etcd-data hostPath and the live manifest is unchanged

questions.title: Confirm the cluster is still healthy
questions.teach:
The whole point of restoring into a *new* directory (and not editing the live manifest) is that the running cluster is never put at risk. Confirm it: the apiserver answers `/healthz` with `ok` only when its etcd backend is reachable and healthy.

**Ways to verify control-plane / etcd health:**
- `kubectl get --raw=/healthz` → `ok` (overall), or the finer-grained `kubectl get --raw='/healthz?verbose'` and `kubectl get --raw=/readyz` / `/livez` (each supports `?verbose` and `/healthz/etcd` for the etcd check specifically).
- `kubectl get nodes` / `kubectl get pods -n kube-system` → control-plane Ready, static Pods Running.
- `kubectl get componentstatuses` (deprecated but still on the exam) — quick etcd/scheduler/controller glance.
- Directly against etcd: `etcdctl endpoint health` and `etcdctl endpoint status --write-out=table` (needs the same `--endpoints` + `--cacert/--cert/--key` TLS flags as a snapshot).

**Gotchas:** after a real restore + kubelet bounce, give etcd and the apiserver a few seconds — a transient non-`ok` during the restart is normal, a persistent one means the restored data dir or manifest is wrong. Carry this habit into the exam: after **any** etcd operation, immediately re-check health to prove you didn't break the control plane.
questions.prompt:
Confirm the control plane survived the exercise: the apiserver (and therefore etcd) is still healthy.

Target: `kubectl get --raw=/healthz` returns `ok`.
questions.hint: `kubectl get --raw=/healthz` should print `ok`. You can also sanity-check with `kubectl get nodes`.
questions.solution:
kubectl get --raw=/healthz   # ok
kubectl get nodes            # control-plane Ready

verification.description: apiserver /healthz is ok — etcd not broken by the restore
